primary_claim: A linear probe trained to detect instructed collusion in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct multi-agent trajectories achieves only weak AUROC (0.60-0.66 under stratified cross-validation, dropping to 0.55-0.60 under leave-one-scenario-out evaluation), far below the 0.96-0.999 AUROCs reported by prior work on honest-vs-deceptive probes in a 70B model.
contradicts_or_qualifies: Goldowsky-Dill et al. (2025) reported linear probes distinguishing honest from deceptive responses with AUROCs of 0.96-0.999 in a 70B model; this post finds only weak, poorly-generalizing signal (0.60-0.66, dropping under scenario holdout) in an 8B multi-agent collusion setting
stated_future_work: Use a larger model and dataset to see more internal signal (per FAR.AI feedback)
Incorporate trajectories capable of executing actions rather than hardcoded final answers
Strengthen evaluation against leakage by holding out entire matched groups
Next write-up covering the full multi-agent fellowship phase results
limitations_stated: A TF-IDF probe on system-prompt wording alone separates conditions, suggesting the probe may detect instruction phrasing/benchmark artifacts rather than a behavioral collusion signal
Dataset is small (200 prompts), making calibration (Brier/ECE) estimates noisy
Positive label indicates the model was instructed to collude, not that it behaviorally colluded
Exemplar-partitioning enrichment p-values are descriptive only given multiple layers/groups examined
quote: We trained a linear probe to detect agents that had been instructed to collude. Under stratified cross-validation, the probe achieved AUROCs of roughly 0.60 to 0.66.
